title: AI's shock-and-awe raid on maths looks like pride before a fall | Rafael Behr
summary: Machines are bulldozing through hard problems to assert the power of their tech bro creators, not to advance human knowledge In most walks of life, trying something 12,363,153,437,138 times and getting the same result is reason enough to assume it works every time. Not in maths, where a conjecture that holds up more than 12tn times looks very probably true but doesn’t qualify as proven. That was the status of the Riemann hypothesis, one of the most famous mathematical conundrums in existence, until last week . Then Levent Alpöge, a mathematician working at Anthropic, said he and his collaborator, Claude AI, had crossed the line from conjecture to proof. title: Dolphins with active social lives and big friendship groups live longer, Australian researchers discover
summary: Decades of data collected at WA’s Shark Bay shows level of socialising may affect longevity for Indo-Pacific bottlenose dolphins Dolphins who spend time socialising in large and consistently sized social groups tend to live longer, new research has found. Indo-Pacific bottlenose dolphins are marine mammals that can live for more than 50 years and have complex social lives. They spend time socialising in groups – which increase in size during their youth and early adulthood, before declining towards the end of their life, according to a study in PLOS Biology. title: China sends first foreign astronaut to ISS rival as it globalises space operations
summary: Muhammad Zeeshan Ali – the first Pakistani to reach orbit – greeted with Chinese ‘space handshake’ at Tiangong station China has flown the first foreign astronaut to its Tiangong space station, starting what it says will be the globalisation of its space operations as the US-led International Space Station (ISS) enters its final years of operation. Floating through a hatch to enter Tiangong, Pakistan’s Muhammad Zeeshan Ali grinned broadly as he was embraced by the onboard crew in what China’s space agency called the country’s first foreign “space handshake”. title: Nasa knocked an asteroid off course. New closeup photos shed light on aftermath
summary: Images of Dimorphos four years on from crash could help scientists design potential planetary defence system Humanity may not yet have a means of fending off a Vogon constructor fleet – the destroyers of Earth in The Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy – but its prospects of surviving an encounter with a rogue asteroid are looking considerably brighter. Four years after Nasa deliberately slammed a spacecraft into a roughly 160-metre-wide asteroid called Dimorphos to knock it off course, scientists have released the first closeup images of the aftermath. title: How a new way of measuring tides could make flood forecasts more accurate
summary: Analysis of differences in tidal height across beaches could lead to more localised tide and flood forecasts The sea might look level, but it turns out tidal height can vary by as much as a metre across the length of a single beach, new research shows. This development is important when it comes to flood predictions and when forecasting which locations are most vulnerable to storm surges. Up until now, our knowledge of tidal levels has been limited. Tide gauges tell us about a specific location, and satellite radar measurements typically average across tens of kilometres. title: Beaver supermoon lights up skylines around the world – video
summary: A stunning supermoon rose over skylines around the world. Supermoons occur when the full moon coincides with the moon being at or near its closest point to Earth, making it appear larger than usual. The November full moon is also known as the beaver moon, a name thought to date to when hunters traditionally set traps for beavers in autumn to secure a supply of warm fur for the winter Continue reading...
